title: Cynefin Framework How to Know Which Kind of Problem Youre Actually Solving
author: The Good Boss
summary: Prompted by a manager whose proven three-step reorg "playbook" mysteriously failed on its third use, this piece introduces the Cynefin Framework, developed by Dave Snowden at IBM in the late 1990s, as a diagnostic for matching leadership response to problem type. Cynefin sorts problems into four domains — Clear (obvious cause and effect, apply best practice), Complicated (cause and effect exist but require expertise to see), Complex (cause and effect only visible in hindsight, the system changes as you act on it), and Chaotic (no time to analyze at all) — and argues each domain calls for a fundamentally different mode of leadership. The manager's reorg failure, in this framing, wasn't a failure of effort but a domain mismatch: a checklist-and-deadline approach suited to Clear or Complicated problems applied to a Complex, people-driven situation. The piece explains why generic leadership advice like "be decisive" is situational rather than universal, since the same trait that makes a leader excel in a crisis can backfire in a complex people problem, and offers a two-minute "Domain Check" technique for diagnosing which domain a problem belongs to before acting.
points: The Cynefin Framework (developed by Dave Snowden at IBM) sorts problems into four domains — Clear, Complicated, Complex, and Chaotic — each requiring a fundamentally different mode of leadership response.

A manager's mistake in the opening anecdote wasn't lack of effort but domain mismatch: applying a checklist-and-deadline playbook (suited to Clear/Complicated problems) to a Complex, people-driven reorg where cause and effect are only visible in hindsight.

Leadership advice like "be decisive" or "build buy-in first" isn't universally right or wrong — it's situational, and the same trait that makes a leader excel in a crisis can backfire in a complex people problem.

The framework is offered as a practical diagnostic ("Domain Check") leaders can run in about two minutes before any significant decision, to identify which domain a problem actually belongs to before choosing a response.
quotes: It wasn't the first time he had managed a reorg. In fact, it was his third time, and he had actually developed a 3-step 'playbook' that he was planning to execute this time.

This time, it took him six weeks to even notice that the plan wasn't working. He later reflected that he was probably trying to solve this problem with a solution that was meant for a different kind of problem.
The core idea behind the framework is that the right response to a problem depends entirely on the habitat that problem lives in, not on how confident or experienced you are.

Complex. In this domain, the cause and the effect are only obvious later, in hindsight. You don't have an expert who can tell you the right answer up front, because the system itself changes as you act on it.

A leader who is great in a crisis situation because he is fast, decisive, and directive, may be a poor leader if thrown into a Complex people problem because there the agility and decisiveness will likely backfire.
Have you noticed how the same manager can look like he's doing a brilliant job with one problem, while being completely clueless with another problem?
